newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-WAUGH PROMOTION PUTS TAYLOR ON PROBATION.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-WAUGH PROMOTION PUTS TAYLOR ON PROBATION.

text.p: Australia captain Mark Taylor will have good reason to look over his shoulder at Steve Waugh during the forthcoming Ashes tour to England.
By promoting Waugh to vice-captain, Australia selectors appear to have sent a clear message to Taylor -- start scoring runs or lose your job.
Faced with Taylor's dismal slump in form this season, the selectors have shown unusual patience by retaining the burly left-handed opener.

But if Taylor's fortunes don't improve, Australia now have a ready-made replacement-in-waiting in Waugh, the country's most experienced cricketer and one of only four current recognised batsman in the world to average more than 50 in test cricket.
Taylor accepted that Waugh could replace him in England during a news conference on Thursday to announce Australia's 17-man tour squad.
"I am a realistic person. That is a possibility," Taylor said in a typically honest response after enduring several weeks of media speculation about his immediate future.
Waugh was elevated at the expense of wicketkeeper Ian Healy, whose reputation was dented when he became the first Australian player to be suspended for dissent.
But Waugh does not regard his promotion as a guarantee of the top job.
"I don't see it as a formality that I'll be captain one day," said the veteran of 89 tests since his debut in 1985-86.
"I've been very happy just playing Test cricket. I really didn't have any inkling I was going to be made vice-captain, but if the chance came along of course I'd love to be captain."
Healy was disciplined for throwing his bat in anger after his dismissal in the third test against South Africa in Pretoria last month.

His demotion suggests selectors were unhappy at the prospect of Healy taking over the captaincy in England if Taylor struggles -- an interpretation that the Queensland player accepted after learning of his fate.
"It's a little bit confusing but I think it's a decision they have now made that the next captain, if Mark fails, will be Stephen and not me," Healy said.
Given his recent poor form, Taylor's survival suggests a relaxation of past selection policy.
Traditionally, an Australian captain has been expected to earn his place, first and foremost, on merit as a player, regardless of his tactical or leadership abilities.
With a test average hovering below 20 this season after a succession of failures at home and in South Africa, Taylor has, on face value, failed to fill that requirement.
Former test fast bowling great Dennis Lillee, for one, argued for Taylor's dismissal on these grounds alone.
"People will always say that at any one time a certain player does not deserve his place in the side," Taylor said.
"But a side is a combination of 11 people and I think I have done my bit in that 11 over the last six months even though I haven't made as many runs as I would have liked."

Further complicating the situation, Australia have thrived during their captain's personal troubles, winning series against West Indies and South Africa to assume the unofficial mantle of test world champions.
In total, Australia have won 15 tests, drawn four and lost eight since since Taylor replaced Allan Border as captain in 1994, including a crushing series win over England at home in 1994-95.
That record appears to have saved Taylor for the time being.
But all that could change if Mike Atherton's struggling England side upset the odds at the start of the Ashes series in June.
